interviewQuestions.question: What is polymorphism really buying you?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The mechanism in one line: calling the same method name on different objects runs each object's own version, decided at runtime. But the mechanism alone isn't the interesting part — the payoff is that callers stop branching on type. Instead of an `if/else` or `instanceof` chain checking every possible type at every call site that needs a shape's area, one call — `shape.area()` — works no matter what's underneath.

I'd make it concrete: with a type-switch chain duplicated across `totalArea`, `drawAll`, and `exportShapes`, adding a `Pentagon` means editing all three call sites, or one of them silently drops it. With polymorphism, adding `Pentagon` means adding one class — no existing call site changes at all. That's Open/Closed in practice: open to new types, closed to modifying existing code.

**Testing:** whether you can name the actual maintenance win, not just define dynamic dispatch and stop there.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Naming the payoff, not just the mechanism

interviewQuestions.question: What's the actual runtime cost of polymorphism — is a vtable lookup something to worry about?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
There's a real cost — one extra indirection through a vtable to find the correct implementation for the object's actual class, versus a direct call resolved at compile time. I wouldn't overstate it, though: in practice this is small, and modern JIT compilers can eliminate it almost entirely in hot loops through inline caching, when the actual type at a given call site turns out to be predictable at runtime.

I'd frame my honest position: it's a real, measurable cost in principle, but it's essentially never the actual bottleneck in real systems — trading away polymorphism's maintainability for a type-switch chain purely on performance grounds is rarely justified without measuring first, and in most codebases the branch-prediction and cache-locality costs of a large if/else chain are comparable anyway.

**Testing:** whether you can name a real cost honestly instead of either dismissing it or treating it as disqualifying.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The real cost of dynamic dispatch

interviewQuestions.question: Does polymorphism require inheritance, or does an interface give you the same benefit?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
An interface gives you the exact same payoff. Callers still get one call site — `shape.area()` — regardless of which concrete implementation sits underneath, and dispatch is still resolved at runtime based on the object's actual type. Inheritance is one common way to set that up, but it's not required; polymorphism is about the dispatch mechanism, not about which language feature happens to provide it.

I'd add that interface-based polymorphism is often preferred in modern practice, specifically because implementing an interface doesn't cost the class its one supertype slot the way extending an abstract class does — you get the identical dispatch benefit at a lower structural cost.

**Testing:** whether you understand polymorphism as a property of dispatch, decoupled from any specific OOP mechanism used to achieve it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Polymorphism without inheritance
